title: A Smile for the Cellar
premise: Cyrus Crane is hired to survey Hollowmere, a decaying estate whose measurements never add up the same way twice. When his daughter Wren arrives unannounced, the house's former inhabitant — her childhood imaginary friend, Marisol — is waiting on the porch, unchanged after twenty years, and recognizes her instantly. Cyrus learns the house sustains itself on a lullaby sung by its heirs: whoever inherits must learn all four verses, and the fourth verse has never been written down, because singing it binds the singer to the cellar forever. As Cyrus's survey becomes a countdown, Wren must choose between finishing the song to free the trapped generations below or breaking the inheritance entirely — and in the end she sings the fourth verse back to the house, reversed, unbinding the dead and leaving Hollowmere to finally measure as empty.
about_author: Jude Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent a decade crawling through the basements of old New England houses before turning to horror. They write in the evenings, always with the doors counted and the lights on.

chapters.title: The Measurements Don't Hold
chapters.summary: Cyrus Crane, a meticulous property surveyor, arrives at Hollowmere to appraise it for the bank. The rooms refuse consistent dimensions; a hallway is four feet longer at dusk. POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: professional unease curdling into the first real fear — the house is not decaying, it is breathing.

chapters.title: Doors, Counted
chapters.summary: Cyrus finds the previous surveyor's notes, obsessively tallying doors: eleven at noon, thirteen by night. He keeps his own count and hears footsteps matching his through the walls, one beat behind. POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: the comfort of ritual as armor, and the dawning sense that the ritual is what the house wants.

chapters.title: A Girl on the Porch
chapters.summary: Wren Crane, twenty-eight and estranged from her father, arrives uninvited to repair their relationship. On the porch sits a small girl in a yellow raincoat, unchanged, who says, 'You came back.' Wren recognizes Marisol, the imaginary friend she invented at Hollowmere as a child. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: vertigo of the impossible made tender.

chapters.title: What Fathers Keep in Basements
chapters.summary: Cyrus hides the cellar from Wren; she finds it anyway. The stairs descend farther than the house is tall. Chalk marks on the walls tally doors in a child's handwriting — her own. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: betrayal braided with wonder; the cellar is where her childhood memories were stored, not made.

chapters.title: The Song Under the Floorboards
chapters.summary: At night, a lullaby rises through the floor — three verses, sung by many voices, thin as paper. Cyrus recognizes it from his own childhood visits to his aunt, the house's last heir. POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: recognition; he was always meant to inherit, and he has been running from it for thirty years.

chapters.title: Marisol's Rules
chapters.summary: Marisol appears only to Wren and speaks in the grammar of a seven-year-old, but her rules are precise: never sing the fourth verse, never answer the cellar, never let the house count you. She cannot say what happens if they break. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: love and dread entwined — Marisol is protector and warden both.

chapters.title: The Heirs' Register
chapters.summary: Cyrus finds the family register in the study: every Crane heir listed, each entry ending in the same date — the day they 'went below.' The last blank line bears his own name, ink already drying. POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: the horror of predestination, of a duty signed before he was asked.

chapters.title: Wren, Counted
chapters.summary: The house begins counting Wren: her reflection arrives late, her footsteps precede her. Marisol grows frantic, insisting they leave before the tally reaches a number she won't name. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: the loss of self by increments; belonging, she realizes, is exactly what the house offers.

chapters.title: Three Verses, Learned
chapters.summary: Cyrus, resigned, decides to learn the song and take the inheritance in Wren's place. The house teaches him willingly — the walls hum the melody, the pipes carry harmony. POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: sacrificial love disguised as duty; he sings along and the house warms to him like a hearth.

chapters.title: The Missing Verse
chapters.summary: The song stops after verse three. Searching the attic, Wren finds a music box with a fourth verse etched inside the lid — scratched out by desperate hands, only the first two notes legible. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: hope sharpened into dread; the cure is also the trap.

chapters.title: Voices Below
chapters.summary: Wren descends the cellar and hears the singers: generations of Cranes, standing in the dark, mouths moving, waiting for someone to finish the verse so they can stop. Her great-aunt recognizes her and begs — in song — for release. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: compassion for the monstrous; the dead are not hungry, they are patient.

chapters.title: Marisol's Origin
chapters.summary: Wren pieces it together: Marisol was a real child, the first heir, who refused the fourth verse and was kept — unaged — as the house's lure for the next generation. Marisol admits it: 'I was your friend so you'd come back.' POV: Wren. Emotional beat: grief for an imaginary friend who was never imaginary, and never free.

chapters.title: The Surveyor's Bargain
chapters.summary: Cyrus offers himself: he will sing the fourth verse, complete the inheritance, if the house releases Wren and the child. The register accepts; the ink on his name darkens. POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: a father's love expressed as a contract he knows is written against him.

chapters.title: Thirteen Doors
chapters.summary: The house's count reaches thirteen doors, and the extra two open onto the cellar and onto Wren's childhood bedroom, perfectly preserved, her small bed turned down as if expected. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: seduction of belonging — the house offers her the childhood she actually wanted.

chapters.title: What the House Wants
chapters.summary: Cyrus, half-belonging now, perceives the house's hunger plainly: it does not want a singer, it wants a family, whole, forever, in the dark. He understands his aunt's smile in old photographs. POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: pity for the predator; the house was once a home that refused to end.

chapters.title: The Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Cyrus practices the fourth verse from the music box's two surviving notes, improvising the rest — but every wrong note makes the cellar singers step closer to the stairs. Marisol covers her ears and weeps. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: terror that love, performed badly, is worse than silence.

chapters.title: The Night of the Open Count
chapters.summary: All thirteen doors stand open at once. The house pulls them toward the cellar like a tide. Cyrus begins the song to hold it; Wren drags Marisol toward the porch. POV: alternating. Emotional beat: the climax's threshold — everything the family is, offered to everything the house is.

chapters.title: The Fourth Verse, Sung Backwards
chapters.summary: At the threshold Wren understands: the verse was never meant to be finished, only returned. She sings the fourth verse in reverse — unbinding rather than binding — and the register's ink runs backward off the page. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: triumph through refusal; the answer to duty is not escape but reversal.

chapters.title: Letting the Dead Measure Out
chapters.summary: The singers ascend the cellar stairs one by one, aging as they climb, and leave through the front door into morning light. The house's rooms settle into honest dimensions. Marisol begins to age too — a girl becoming a ghost becoming nothing. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: release that costs everything; freeing the dead means freeing her friend.

chapters.title: Marisol's Last Afternoon
chapters.summary: Marisol spends one human afternoon on the porch with Wren — real sunlight, real hunger, a real goodbye. 'You were the only one who made me up,' she says, 'so only you could let me down.' POV: Wren. Emotional beat: the book's heart — love against duty, kept past the end.

chapters.title: The Final Survey
chapters.summary: Cyrus completes the survey: eleven doors, every room true, the cellar measuring as shallow dirt and old stone. He files the report recommending demolition. Father and daughter leave together, neither looking back at the porch. POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: quiet reconciliation; the duty he finally keeps is to the living.

chapters.title: A Smile for the Cellar
chapters.summary: Epilogue: demolition day. As the walls come down, workers find nothing in the cellar but a child's yellow raincoat, folded neatly, and a chalk tally on the stone — eleven doors, then a final mark: zero. Wren, watching from the road, smiles and does not sing. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: bittersweet closure; the house is ended, the belonging was real, and it goes with them.
